blocks.text: Genesis 5 uses a steady genealogical pattern: each man fathers a named son, continues to have other children, lives a stated total number of years, and usually ends with the words “and he died.” The pattern carries the line from Adam through Seth toward Noah. Its opening also links Adam’s creation in God’s likeness with Seth’s birth in Adam’s likeness and image.

The chapter is more than a sequence of ages. It maintains an unbroken line from Adam to Noah while repeatedly emphasizing human mortality. Enoch interrupts the usual pattern: he “walked with God” and was taken by God rather than receiving the ordinary death notice. At the chapter’s close, Lamech explains Noah’s name through his hope for relief from labor and pain connected with the cursed ground. These features suggest that the genealogy advances the narrative and its themes, rather than presenting itself as an explicit modern chronology table.

Genesis 5 belongs to Genesis 1–11, which may be read as ancient theological and literary discourse rather than forced into modern scientific genres or dismissed as merely decorative myth. Comparisons with other ancient Near Eastern traditions can illuminate shared motifs and questions, but such parallels alone do not prove direct copying or settle how Genesis should be interpreted.
